newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan opposition tightens net on Taleban in north.
newsitem.headline: Afghan opposition tightens net on Taleban in north.

text.p: Opposition forces were closing in on a Taleban force stranded in the town of Pul-i-Khumri in northern Afghanistan on Monday, Taleban fighters said.
They said the Taleban had retreated on front lines north and south of the town, about 160 km (100 miles) north of Kabul.
The Islamic militia ceded the town of Doshi, 46 km (29 miles) south of Pul-i-Khumri, to forces loyal to Syed Jafar Naderi, who lost Pul-i-Khumri to the Taleban on Wednesday.

"Doshi has been captured by Syed Jafar's militia. There was no fighting there. We were ordered to pull back by our leaders," a Taleban commander, Mohammed Gul Niazi, told reporters on Monday at his position close to the new front line, about 30 km (19 miles) south of Pul-i-Khumri.
He said pro-Taleban forces were holding out on the other side of Doshi, adding that Jafar's Ismaili militia controlled only a one-km (1,000-yard) stretch of road.
The Taleban also lost ground north of Pul-i-Khumri, where they are facing opposition forces loyal to the mainly Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat militia, a Taleban tank commander said.

"The front line has moved back to the village of Arobotak. It was a tactical withdrawal. We were not forced out," said commander Habibullah (one name). He said his forces would launch an offensive in the next few days to retake the lost territory.
The new northern front line is some 35 km (22 miles) from Pul-i-Khumri, a Taleban loss of some 15 km (nine miles).
The Taleban moved into north Afghanistan two weeks ago when an opposition commander, General Abdul Malik, defected and joined their ranks.
They moved across the north, meeting little opposition, to take the northern capital of Mazar-i-Sharif.
But their victory was short-lived. Four days after taking
Mazar-i-Sharif, Malik turned on his new allies and drove them out of the city in fierce street battles in which at least 100 people were killed.

As the debacle in Mazar-i-Sharif was unfolding, Taleban forces were moving north from Kabul, overcoming obstacles that included a collapsed bridge and a stretch of tunnel that had been blown up, to cross the Hindu Kush mountain range and roll north into Pul-i-Khumri.
Their problems in Pul-i-Khumri started when the road from Kabul, their main supply route, was cut by opposition guerrillas led by former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.

The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press reported on Monday that a key Masood commander in the Salang area, Basir Salangi, whose defection on May 25 allowed the Taleban column to cross the towering mountain pass, had again switched loyalties.
"He changed sides yesterday or the day before and is now fighting against the Taleban," AIP said.
Surrounded, outnumbered and short of heavy weapons, the Taleban force north of the Salang has been compelled to retreat into an ever-diminishing enclave centred around Pul-i-Khumri.
